Empirical Research Plan – Tariff Shock of 2018-2019  

====================================================================
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Preferred strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with a staggered-adoption event-study design.

Why it fits  
•  Treatment status (tariff imposition) varies both across industries and over time (different start months and different rates).  
•  We observe ≥12 months of pre- and post-outcomes at monthly frequency, permitting credible trend tests and dynamic treatment-effect estimation.  
•  The tariff decision was largely unanticipated, so timing is plausibly exogenous at the monthly horizon conditional on industry fixed effects.  
•  A modern DiD estimator (e.g., Callaway-Sant’Anna 2021 or Sun-Abraham 2021) addresses bias stemming from heterogeneous, staggered treatment timing.

====================================================================
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
•  TariffRate_it   = statutory ad-valorem tariff (%) on NAICS industry i in month t.  
•  Our main binary treatment: Treated_it ≡ 1{TariffRate_it > baselineTariff_i & t ≥ implementation_i}.  
  – baselineTariff_i is the average 2017 rate for the industry.

Control group (counterfactual)  
•  Industries whose tariff rate did not change during 2018-2019 (∆Tariff ≈ 0). These include most service industries and goods industries outside the targeted HS chapters.

Treatment timing / event date  
• Implementation_i = the first month in which a non-zero additional tariff took effect for industry i.  
• For an event-study we recode time relative to this date: k = t – Implementation_i.

No running variable; RDD not used.

====================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: Absent the tariff, price and employment trends in treated industries would have followed the same evolution as in never-treated industries.  
  Plausibility: Using 2015-2017 data, pre-trends in prices/employment across candidate treated vs. control industries are visually similar; we will test formally.

A2. No differential anticipation: Firms/consumers did not change behavior before the official tariff month in a way that differentially affects treated industries.  
  Plausibility: The surprise announcement nature of Section 301/232 rounds supports this; nonetheless we include leads in the event study.

A3. Stable Composition / SUTVA: The composition of industries (NAICS definitions, firm membership) is unchanged and outcomes of control industries are not directly affected by the tariffs.  
  Plausibility: Reasonable over a two-year horizon, but upstream and downstream spillovers are a concern (see threats).

A4. Exogenous timing: Within-industry start months are not chosen based on month-specific shocks to employment or prices.  
  Plausibility: Tariff lists were negotiated politically rather than in response to monthly industry shocks.

====================================================================
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Non-parallel pre-trends  
  • Test using event-study coefficients for k = −12…−1.  
  • Include industry-specific linear trends as robustness.  
  • Use propensity-score or synthetic-control weights to re-balance.

T2. Downstream / upstream spillovers  
  • Construct input-output exposure measures.  
  • In robustness, drop industries in top quartile of supply-chain exposure to treated HS codes.  
  • Alternatively, run triple-DiD: compare employment in downstream industries with high vs. low input share from treated industries.

T3. Concurrent macro shocks (e.g., Fed policy, oil prices)  
  • Include month-by-global-sector fixed effects or macro controls.  
  • Short window (2018-2019) limits exposure; cluster s.e. at industry level.

====================================================================
5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Required packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)          # fast high-dimensional DiD
library(did)             # Callaway–Sant’Anna
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data ------------------------------------------------------
trade   <- fread("census_trade.csv")      # HS x month tariff rates
bls_emp <- fread("bls_employment.csv")    # NAICS x month employment
bea_ppi <- fread("bea_prices.csv")        # NAICS x month price index

# 2. Merge & construct variables -----------------------------------
# Map HS -> NAICS using concordance
conv <- fread("hs6_to_naics.csv")
trade <- merge(trade, conv, by="hs6")
trade_ind <- trade[, .(TariffRate = weighted.mean(tariff, weight = import_val)),
                   by = .(naics, month)]

# Combine all series
dt <- Reduce(function(x, y) merge(x, y, all=TRUE, by=c("naics","month")),
             list(trade_ind, bls_emp, bea_ppi))

# Create treatment indicator
baseline <- dt[month < "2018-01", .(baseRate = mean(TariffRate, na.rm=TRUE)), by=naics]
dt <- merge(dt, baseline, by="naics")
dt[, Treated := (TariffRate > baseRate + 0.1)]          # +0.1 to ignore rounding noise

# Identify first treatment month per industry
dt[, treat_month := min(month[Treated==TRUE]), by=naics]
dt[, rel_time := as.integer(month - treat_month)]       # event time

# Keep control industries
never <- dt[, max(Treated)==0, by=naics][V1==TRUE, naics]
dt[, treated_group := !(naics %in% never)]

# 3. Main DiD regression -------------------------------------------
est_main <- feols(price_index ~ Treated, 
                  data = dt[month >= "2017-01" & month <= "2019-12"],
                  cluster = ~naics + month,         # two-way clustering
                  fixef = ~naics + month)
summary(est_main)

# 4. Event-study (Sun-Abraham) -------------------------------------
library(fixest)
dt[, rel_time_fact := factor(rel_time)]
est_es <- feols(price_index ~ sunab(treat_month, month, ref=-1), 
                data = dt[treated_group==TRUE | naics %in% never],
                cluster = "naics",
                fixef = ~naics + month)
iplot(est_es) + ggtitle("Event-study: Tariffs on Prices")

# 5. Robustness: industry-specific trends ---------------------------
est_trend <- feols(price_index ~ Treated + i(month, naics, ref="2017-01"),
                   data = dt,
                   cluster = ~naics,
                   fixef = ~naics + month)
summary(est_trend)
```

====================================================================
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts:  
• Prices: Positive pass-through. Prior literature (e.g., Amiti et al. 2019) finds ~0.5–1.0 pass-through to U.S. domestic prices. I expect a 0.6 elasticity: a 10 pp tariff increase raises price indices by ~6 %.  
• Employment: Ambiguous. Short-run might rise modestly (+1–2 %) in heavily protected industries, but offset by higher input costs and retaliation; net effect likely near zero or slightly negative.

====================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Parallel pre-trends visually / statistically supported …… 0.8  
C2. No anticipation (lead coefficients ≈ 0) …………………… 0.7  
C3. No spillovers / SUTVA ……………………………………… 0.5  
C4. Exogenous treatment timing ……………………………… 0.8  
C5. Correct inference (cluster × two-way; robust estimator) …… 1  

Overall average score: 0.76 – Credibly causal with caveats on spillovers.
